doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

chapter: Swing, hot jazz and the bebop split
title: Hot jazz, trad, and the split with bebop
summary: He defines hot jazz, recalls the mixed playlists of 1940s disc jockeys, and criticizes the notion of progress and the dismissal of older players.

bands.name: Jack Bland and His Rhythm Makers

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: When we’re talking definitions, when I look at your CDs and the kind of music you do, is there a way you can describe “trad jazz” and “hot?” When you use the word “hot” you know was hot, did that mean jazz too?

Yes. Hot jazz, as opposed to cool jazz. I think it’s just a physical thing. I mean certain people like to live in Spain, certain people like to live in Vermont. I mean people make a lot of this. There is room for all of them. I happen to have been weaned, early on, not only on Louis Armstrong and Bix Beiderbecke and Bessie Smith and Duke Ellington, of course. When I was just thirteen and fourteen it was wonderful in New York particularly because we had disc jockeys, jazz disc jockeys, who didn’t, who were very catholic in their tastes. I use the word not in the religious sense, the other sense. I mean you’d hear Erroll Garner’s first recording, “White Rose Bounce” or one of those things, and the next tune would be Jack Bland and his Rhythm Makers, and the next tune would be Duke Ellington’s “Main Stem,” and the next tune might be Bessie Smith. So you had this whole mish mosh. And I never — and a Benny Goodman sextet thing followed by Lester Young with Johnny Guanieri and Slam Stewart and Sid Catlett followed by Bix Beiderbecke and his gang, I mean it was like that. And so it was only later on that that separation came. That came during the bebop era, through the efforts of guys like Leonard Feather and stuff, to somehow, you know, call the old stuff is crappy. And frankly, I don’t know if I’m answering your question, but I find the notion of progress in music spurious. There is change of course, but whether you can say that Alban Berg is per se better than Johann Bach, you know, than Bach, I mean it’s different. It came later. It’s got a thing of this, and this, and this is the way I feel about it. But at that time there was somehow this division between squares and moldy figs, and boppers, and those who were hip you know and it was a terrible thing. All of a sudden, guys who, life is short, and in twenty years had gotten their art to a form of perfection, guys like Bud Freeman or Buck Clayton or Teddy Wilson or something, all of a sudden they were sort of passé.

You know they’re forty years old and they’re passé. Ridiculous. Ridiculous. What do they want from a guy? That he change his colors every five years which way the wind blows, all of a sudden you become a Stan Kenton, you change from— So anyway—
Was it mostly the non-musicians that started that? Was it the writers and the critics?
